lead: A normal form is a promise about the shape of every production. Chomsky normal form allows only A → BC or A → a. Greibach normal form allows only A → aα. The promise removes cases from proofs and algorithms: a check on a rule has two or three shapes, not dozens. CYK membership needs CNF (see 3.8). PDA to CFG conversions use the GNF idea (see Unit 4, Pushdown Automata). CNF covers every context-free language; GNF covers every context-free language without ε, and Section 3 shows how ε is handled. A converted grammar can be larger than the one you started with.
prereq: You need the simplification steps from 3.4: removing useless symbols, ε rules and unit rules.

sections.h3: Chomsky normal form: two rule shapes

blocks.text: Write variables as capital letters A, B, S and terminals as lowercase a, b. A context-free grammar is in Chomsky normal form (CNF) when every production has one of two shapes: A → BC, with exactly two variables on the right, or A → a, with exactly one terminal. There are no unit rules A → B and no ε rules, with one exception: S → ε is allowed if the start variable S never appears on the right side of any rule. That exception lets the grammar generate the empty string without breaking the two shapes.

The conversion starts from the simplified grammar of 3.4. First, for every terminal a that appears in a right side of length two or more, add a new variable and replace a by it. A rule A → aB becomes A → C B and C → a. A rule A → ab becomes A → C D, C → a, D → b, because two terminals are not allowed. Second split every right side of length three or more. For A → BCDE, introduce a fresh variable X and write A → B X and X → CDE. Then split X → CDE with another fresh variable Y: X → C Y and Y → D E. The figure shows the same split on the worked example’s rule S → A S B, which becomes S → A X and X → S B. Third check for unit rules as a safety step. Splitting never introduces a unit rule: every rule it produces has two variables on the right. Unit rules are removed during simplification (3.4), before terminal replacement and splitting. The result has only the two allowed shapes.

items: A → B is a unit rule and is not CNF.
Simplify the grammar: remove useless symbols, ε rules and unit rules (3.4). Keep S → ε only if S is absent from all right sides.
For each terminal a that appears in a right side of length two or more, add a new variable T with rule T → a, and replace a by T in those long right sides.

For each rule A → X₁X₂...Xₖ with k ≥ 3, introduce fresh variables and split from the left: A → X₁ Z₁, Z₁ → X₂ Z₂, and so on until the last rule has two symbols. For A → BCDE this can be written A → B X, X → CDE, then X → C Y, Y → D E.
Remove unit rules by substituting the right side of B into A → B. Repeat until no unit rule remains.
If ε is in the language and S → ε was kept, ensure S does not appear on any right side. Rename variables if needed.

blocks.text: Splitting adds one variable and one production per extra symbol. Terminal replacement adds one variable and one production per terminal used in long rules. The grammar grows, often to about twice the original size, but every rule now has the CNF shape.

sections.h3: Greibach normal form: every rule starts with a terminal

blocks.text: Greibach normal form (GNF) allows only productions A → aα, where a is one terminal and α is a string of variables, possibly empty. Every step of a derivation therefore writes a terminal first. GNF grammars have no ε rules and no unit rules. If the language contains ε, GNF is usually stated for the language without ε, or a separate start rule is added outside the form.

Order the variables A₁, ..., Aₙ. Rewrite rules so that Aᵢ → Aⱼα only when j > i. For a rule that starts with a lower or equal index, substitute the rules of that variable. A rule Aᵢ → Aᵢα is immediate left recursion; remove it with standard left-recursion removal, which introduces a new variable. After the ordering is clean, expand the first variable of each right side repeatedly until a terminal appears at the front. Every expansion replaces a leading variable by its rules, so the process ends with A → aα.

Take S → AB, A → aA | a, B → bB | b. Substitute A's rules into S → AB: S → aAB | aB. The rules A → aA | a and B → bB | b already start with terminals. Every rule now starts with one terminal followed by variables, so the grammar is in GNF.

spec.aria: Three boxes of rules from S → aSb | ab to the final CNF grammar, and below, the tree S → A S B split into S → A X with X → S B.

examples.question: Convert the grammar G: S → aSb | ab to Chomsky normal form. State the final grammar and count its productions.
steps: The grammar has no ε rules and no unit rules. Both symbols are useful.
Add A → a and B → b. Replace terminals inside right sides of length two or more. S → aSb becomes S → A S B. S → ab becomes S → A B.
Split S → A S B. It has three symbols. Introduce X: S → A X and X → S B.
The rule S → A B already has two variables. The rule X → S B has two variables. A → a and B → b have one terminal.
No unit rule was created. The start S appears on the right in X → S B, but there is no S → ε, so the exception is not needed.
Final CNF grammar: S → A X | A B, X → S B, A → a, B → b. It has 5 productions.
examples.answer: The CNF grammar is S → A X | A B, X → S B, A → a, B → b; it has 5 productions.

traps: A → aB is not CNF. A terminal and a variable on the right is not one of the two shapes.
A → BCD must be split into binary rules. Leaving three variables on the right is not CNF.
Do not drop the S → ε exception when ε is in the language. Also do not allow any other ε rule.
In GNF, A → aBc is not allowed: after the first terminal, only variables may follow, so c must be replaced by a variable.

Splitting never introduces a unit rule; every rule it produces has two variables on the right. Unit rules are removed during simplification (3.4), before terminal replacement and splitting; check again at the end only as a precaution.

quiz.q: State the two allowed shapes of a production in Chomsky normal form.
quiz.a: A → BC with two variables, or A → a with one terminal. No unit rules, no ε rules except possible S → ε.

quiz.q: Why does CNF forbid A → aB?
quiz.a: CNF fixes the right side to either two variables or one terminal. A mixed terminal-variable rule would add a third case to every proof and algorithm, so conversion replaces a by a new variable.

quiz.q: Convert S → aS | b to CNF.
quiz.a: Add A → a. Replace a in S → aS: S → A S. S → b is already one terminal. No unit rule. CNF: S → A S | b, A → a.

quiz.q: Why can a GNF grammar not generate ε, apart from a separate start exception?
quiz.a: Every GNF production A → aα writes at least one terminal. A derivation of ε would need a production that writes nothing, which GNF does not allow.

quiz.q: Put S → AB, A → aA | a, B → bB | b into GNF.
quiz.a: Substitute A's rules into S → AB: S → aAB | aB. A and B rules already start with terminals. GNF: S → aAB | aB, A → aA | a, B → bB | b.

quiz.q: Why is A → BCDE split as A → BX, X → CY, Y → DE rather than A → BC, D → DE?
quiz.a: The split must keep the original order B C D E. A → BC would drop D and E, and D → DE is a separate rule that cannot be reached. Fresh variables carry the remaining suffix.

quiz.q: What is the shape of a Greibach normal form production?
quiz.a: A → aα, where a is one terminal and α is a string of variables, possibly empty.

quiz.q: Why do normal forms make proofs about context-free grammars shorter?
quiz.a: A proof can check two or three rule shapes instead of arbitrary right sides. This reduces case analysis in induction on derivation length or parse tree height.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern parser generators often rewrite grammars into binary form internally, close to CNF, because binary rules make table filling cheaper. GNF appears in theoretical constructions from a CFG to a pushdown automaton that reads one terminal per move. Grammar size can blow up under these conversions, so tools often keep the original grammar and use specialised algorithms. Search for “Chomsky normal form CYK” and “Greibach normal form pushdown automaton” to go further.
